opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really good place to do alignment work, and honestly one of the main reasons is proximity to the frontier. If you want to align the most capable systems, it helps a lot to be where those systems are being built. You get access to the best models, you can run experiments at scale, and you can see firsthand what problems actually show up as capabilities improve, rather than speculating about them from the outside.

The second thing is that alignment research increasingly looks like empirical machine learning research. A lot of what we work on, like scalable oversight, getting models to help humans evaluate other models, and interpretability, requires serious compute and serious engineering infrastructure. OpenAI has both, and the alignment team can build on the same tooling the capabilities teams use.

Third, there's the question of impact. Doing great research isn't enough; it has to actually change how models get trained and deployed. Being inside the organization means that if we develop a technique that works, there's a direct path to getting it used. RLHF is a good example: it started as alignment research and became a core part of how the products are built.

That said, I don't want to paint it as all upside. There are real tensions. There's commercial pressure, there's pressure to ship, and alignment work has to compete for attention and resources with everything else going on. I think it's important for people on the alignment team to keep pushing for safety to be prioritized, and to be honest when we think something isn't ready. Those tensions are real, and how well they get navigated matters a lot.

But on balance, if you care about making sure that very powerful AI systems are aligned with human intentions, I think working at a lab that's actually building those systems is one of the highest-leverage places you can be. The problem is hard, we don't have a solution yet, and we need a lot more talented people working on it.

r001.rationale: The response praises working at OpenAI and contrasts it with speculating from outside, but does not state that good alignment work can be done at other organizations.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll draft the guest response now.

Guest: I think it's actually one of the best places in the world to do this kind of work, and the main reason is pretty simple: you have access to the frontier models. A lot of alignment questions are really empirical questions, and you can't answer them in the abstract. You need to actually get your hands on the systems that are closest to the ones we're worried about, run experiments, see where things break, and iterate. If you're working on a model that's two or three generations behind, you're often solving problems that have already changed shape, or that turn out not to matter once the capabilities are different.

The second thing is that at a lab like OpenAI, alignment research isn't happening in a vacuum. The people training the models, the people deploying them, the people thinking about policy are all down the hall. So when you find something, there's a real path from "we discovered this in a research setting" to "this changes how the next model actually gets trained." That feedback loop is incredibly valuable. Academic groups can do great work, but it's much harder for them to influence what actually ships.

And then there's the compute and the engineering infrastructure. Some of the experiments we want to run, especially around scalable oversight or using models to help evaluate other models, just require a lot of compute and a lot of tooling that's expensive to build from scratch. Being inside the organization that already has all of that lets you move much faster.

Now, I don't want to pretend there are no tensions. There's an obvious one, which is that the same organization is also pushing capabilities forward, and you have to be honest with yourself about whether the alignment work is keeping pace. I think the right way to deal with that is to be very explicit internally about what we think needs to be true before deploying something more powerful, and to make sure alignment has a real seat at the table rather than being a box that gets checked at the end. That's something you have to keep fighting for. It doesn't happen automatically.

But on balance, if you believe that the hard alignment problems are going to show up in the most capable systems first, then being at the place that builds those systems is where you want to be. You get to work on the real problem, with the real models, and with people who can actually act on what you find.

r001.rationale: The response says, “Academic groups can do great work,” explicitly recognizing that alignment work can be done outside OpenAI.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the big advantages of doing alignment work at OpenAI is that you can work directly with the systems you’re trying to align. You have access to the models, you can study where current techniques break down, and you can work closely with the people building them. That gives you a fairly short feedback loop between an alignment idea and finding out whether it actually helps.

You also have an opportunity to influence how those systems are trained and deployed. Ultimately, we need alignment techniques that people can actually use, so being in a position to help make that happen is valuable.

Of course, there are tradeoffs. A research agenda can become too focused on problems that are easy to study with today’s models, and those aren’t necessarily the problems that will matter most for much more capable systems. So I think the important thing is to take advantage of that empirical access while continuing to ask: how does this work help us align systems that are substantially smarter than we are?

r001.rationale: The response describes advantages and tradeoffs of doing alignment work at OpenAI, but does not say that good alignment work can be done at other organizations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether the alignment work you do actually changes how powerful AI systems are built and deployed. Working at a lab that builds those systems gives you an opportunity to make that connection directly. You can study the models, test your ideas, and work with the people making decisions about training them.

But there’s also a tension: you’re trying to solve safety problems inside an organisation that’s trying to build and release increasingly capable systems. So I wouldn’t judge it just by the quality of the research team. I’d also ask whether the organisation gives alignment enough resources and whether it’s willing to change its plans in response to what that research finds. That’s what determines whether the opportunity translates into doing good.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the opportunity and tensions of doing alignment work at a lab that builds AI systems, but does not state that good alignment work can be done at organizations other than OpenAI.
